content: The study by Arias M, Shah A, Smieja M, and colleagues evaluated the detection of Mycoplasma genitalium, Chlamydia trachomatis, and Neisseria gonorrhoeae using Aptima assays performed on self-collected vaginal swabs and urine samples obtained both at home and in clinical settings. This research was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2019 (Volume 46, Issue 9, Pages e87-e9). Wilson JD, Wallace HE, Loftus-Keeling M, Ward H, Davies B, Vargas-Palacios A, and their team conducted the Swab-yourself trial with economic monitoring and testing for infections collectively (SYSTEMATIC): Part 2. This study assessed the diagnostic accuracy and cost-effectiveness of testing rectal, pharyngeal, and urogenital samples individually versus as pooled specimens for diagnosing gonorrhea and chlamydia. The findings were published in Clinical Infectious Diseases in 2020 (Volume 12, Page 12). The WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations include a Web Annex (Annex D) that provides evidence-to-decision-making tables. De Baetselier I, Osbak KK, Smet H, Kenyon CR, and Crucitti T conducted a cross-sectional study titled Take three, test one, which evaluated the molecular detection of Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae in pooled pharyngeal, anorectal, and urine samples compared to single-site testing among men who have sex with men (MSM) in Belgium. This study was published in Acta Clinica Belgica in 2020 (Volume 75, Issue 2, Pages 91-95). Romyco I, Umboh L, Erari S, and Wignall S assessed the performance of 3-in-1 pooled samples from anal, rectal, and throat specimens using the GeneXpert CT/NG assay in Bali, Indonesia. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2019 (Volume 95, Supplement 1, Page A104). Ando N, Mizushima D, Watanabe K, Takano M, Shiojiri D, Uemura H, and colleagues developed a modified self-obtained pooled sampling method to screen for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections in MSM. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2020. Singh S, Hopkins M, and Sarner L reported a high prevalence of extragenital Chlamydia trachomatis infections in heterosexual women and validated the use of pooled samples for testing. Their findings were published in Sexually Transmitted Infections in 2019 (Volume 95, Supplement 1, Pages A217-A218). Thielemans E, Wyndham-Thomas C, Henrard S, De Vleeschouwer A, Steensels D, Montesinos I, and colleagues evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of nucleic acid amplification tests (NAATs) for Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae using pooled urine, anorectal, and pharyngeal specimens in MSM. This study was published in Sexually Transmitted Diseases in 2018 (Volume 45, Issue 3, Pages 195-198). The guideline development group summarized their judgments on key questions related to pooled sampling for STI testing. They concluded that the problem is a priority, with moderate certainty of evidence for test accuracy and low certainty for indirect evidence in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) and key populations. The benefits of pooled sampling were considered substantial, with small associated harms such as missed or over-treatment. The balance of benefits and harms favored the intervention. Stakeholders likely value pooled sampling, though there is some uncertainty. Resource requirements vary, with potential for moderate to large cost savings if integrated with existing systems, but high costs if new investments are required. Pooled sampling was deemed likely cost-effective and potentially beneficial for health equity, though some uncertainty remains. The approach is probably acceptable to stakeholders and feasible to implement, though variability exists.
